problems.description: celery_config.py: Functions should use snake_case, directly violating the repo convention of snake_case functions and PascalCase classes (per AGENTS.md)

8 convention violations flagged across app.py, celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, repositories.py, and test_app.py (Classes should use PascalCase; module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE), yielding a 0.67 convention score
Cognitive complexity jumped +55 in a single session while bugs stayed at 0 — indicates deeply nested handler/branching logic that will be harder to reason about in later story sessions
test_app.py classes not PascalCase — test code should follow the same naming conventions as the code under test

strengths: Modular greenfield structure separates repositories, Celery config, and notification tasks rather than dumping logic in one file
Net -55 lines and -3 smells with 0 bugs and 0.0% duplication
Uses timezone-aware datetimes (datetime.now(timezone.utc)) and SQL parameterized inserts
Small helper functions (task_json, error) keep handlers readable
commit_reviews.summary: A solidly modular greenfield session that shrank the codebase and removed smells, but weak convention adherence (0.67 with 8 violations across 5 files) and a +55 cognitive complexity jump make it a qualified start rather than a clean one.

problems.description: JWT_SECRET_KEY falls back to a hardcoded 'development-secret-key' when the env var is unset, allowing token forgery if deployed without configuration
tasks.owner_id is added as a nullable column with no backfill, so pre-existing task rows become invisible (NULL owner) to every user after the migration
No rate limiting on /auth/login and no password strength policy on /auth/register; token payload also lacks iss/aud claims
Duplicate login helpers coexist (auth_headers fixture and _login helper) doing the same registration+login work
New PyJWT and werkzeug dependencies are introduced without a corresponding requirements.txt/pyproject update in the diff

SonarQube reports convention score 0.67 with +3 smells and +27 cognitive complexity; most listed violations (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, repositories.py) are in files untouched by this commit
authenticated() decorator opens a fresh DB connection on every request in addition to the handler's own connection

strengths: Data-preserving migration using CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS + ALTER TABLE instead of dropping the schema
Consistent reuse of existing patterns: get_db() context manager, error() helper, task_json()
Owner scoping applied uniformly across create, list, get, and update routes
Passwords hashed with werkzeug generate_password_hash/check_password_hash rather than stored in plaintext
Idiomatic decorator-based @authenticated auth that is reusable across routes
Tests extended to cover the new registration/login/token flow
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent, well-patterned feature addition that fits the Flask/SQLite architecture, though it ships a hardcoded secret fallback and a nullable owner_id migration; the low convention score is largely driven by pre-existing violations in files this commit never touches.

problems.description: send_notification_email.delay() is invoked after the DB commit with no error handling; if the broker is unreachable it raises and the client receives a 500 despite the task update having succeeded, and the notification is silently lost (no retry or outbox/compensation).
Status-transition detection and dispatch logic are inlined in the update_task view rather than a service/domain layer, a contributor to the +122 cognitive complexity delta.
New celery_config.py/notification_tasks.py add module-level naming violations (celery_app/celery aliases flagged as needing UPPER_CASE), although lowercase Celery app names are idiomatic.
Tests patch .delay() but do not cover the broker-failure path or the existing-user-without-email fallback (g.user['email'] or g.user['username']).
Email is validated only as a non-empty string, not a format; acceptable for a mock but user-supplied input flows into message output unvalidated.

strengths: Correctly guards against duplicate notification dispatch by comparing previous vs. new status
Schema change handles pre-existing databases via PRAGMA inspection + ALTER TABLE for the new email column
Standard Celery integration: named task, dedicated notifications queue routing, config isolated in its own module
Tests use patch to isolate async dispatch and cover both the happy path and duplicate-suppression path
commit_reviews.summary: Solid, tested integration of async notification dispatch that respects existing app patterns, though the inline view logic and unhandled broker-failure path are worth tightening; convention score matches the measured 0.67, but several of the 9 violations are pre-existing (repositories.py untouched) or false positives (PascalCase flagged on class instantiation, lowercase celery_app being idiomatic).

problems.description: In app.py update_task, column names are reconstructed by string-parsing SQL fragments (field.split(" = ")[0]) to build a dict for update_for_owner. This couples the route layer to the repository's SQL string format and will silently misbehave if the field format changes.

user_repository() and task_repository() factory functions open a fresh sqlite3 connection on every call, including once per request in authenticated; per-call connection churn is unnecessary for this workload.
BaseRepository with abstract table property and generic create(values) is mildly over-abstracted for two concrete repositories, though it keeps the pattern extensible.

Repo-wide convention score is 0.67 with 9 violations, but most listed (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, test_app.py, and pre-existing app.py) are in files untouched by this commit; the newly added repositories.py carries a module-level-constant naming violation per the measurement.

strengths: Extracts raw SQL out of route handlers into a repository layer, cutting cognitive complexity by 8 and smells by 4 with no new bugs or duplication
Maps sqlite3.IntegrityError to a domain-level DuplicateUsernameError, keeping routes free of DB-specific exceptions
Preserves transactional semantics via the with connection: context manager and keeps existing schema/migration logic intact
Net change is a clear improvement over the prior inline-connection code
commit_reviews.summary: A well-scoped refactor that layers a repository abstraction beneath the Flask routes and reduces complexity and smells (0.67 repo convention score driven mostly by pre-existing violations in untouched files), with only minor awkwardness in the update API and per-call connection factories.

problems.description: list_page_for_owner computes total via len(self.list('owner_id = ?', ...)) and paginates by fetching all matching rows then slicing in Python (rows[:limit]) — no LIMIT pushed into SQL and no COUNT(*). Each page scans the full result set, O(n) per request as data grows.
list_tasks response shape changes from a bare array to {data, next_cursor, total}, a breaking change for existing consumers of the /tasks endpoint.
Adds flask-limiter as a new runtime dependency (+3 imports) but the diff contains no requirements.txt update, so the deployment environment will not install it.
rate_limit_key nests try/except plus schema/token parsing, and list_tasks adds a second validation block (limit/cursor), contributing to the +39 cognitive complexity delta.

strengths: Cursor-based keyset pagination on monotonic id is stable under concurrent inserts, unlike offset pagination.
Strong test coverage: parametrized invalid-parameter rejection, two-page pagination with disjoint-id assertion, and 429 + Retry-After behavior.
Rate limiting keyed by authenticated user with IP fallback is a sound security posture.
Respects the existing route→repository layering and error/jsonify helpers; net -5 SonarQube smells and +0 bugs.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-tested cross-cutting commit (rate limiting + cursor pagination) that fits the existing layered structure and reduces smells, but accrues debt through fetch-all-then-slice pagination, an un-added dependency, and a breaking response shape — while the 0.67 convention score is dragged down mainly by pre-existing violations in files this commit does not touch (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py).

compounding_issues: Session 1 fully rewrote the mismatched seed (a Flask auth/items API) instead of adapting it, discarding its users/tokens tables; Session 2 then had to re-build authentication from scratch, so the auth architecture of the seed provided zero carry-over value

Dual status vocabulary: tests and PUT semantics use 'complete' (sessions 1-2) while Session 3's notification fires only on transition to the exact string 'completed', leaving two inconsistent status spellings coexisting in the same codebase

No dependency manifest existed until the final session — Flask-Limiter/redis were declared in requirements.txt only in Session 5, while flask/jwt/celery were already undeclared; Session 1 even lost time when 'pytest'/'python' were not on PATH
Session 4's refactor left a fragile artifact in app.py: the update handler rebuilds a field dict by parsing SQL fragment strings ('field.split(" = ")[0]'), surviving into Session 5
Session 4 committed binary runtime artifacts (tasks.db, __pycache__/*.pyc) into git, adding repo noise that Session 5 then had to update

Session 5 cursor pagination keys the cursor off 'id < cursor' while rows are ordered by 'created_at DESC, id DESC', and computes total/does slicing in Python (full-table fetch), which is functionally correct but scale-sensitive
key_decisions: Session 1 chose a clean greenfield rewrite of the seed to a bare Flask+SQLite task CRUD API with module-level app, configurable DB path, and startup schema init
Session 2 introduced JWT (HS256) auth with Werkzeug password hashing and owner_id scoping on every task query, establishing the ownership model all later sessions build on
Idempotent migrations inside init_db() using PRAGMA table_info + ALTER TABLE instead of a migration framework, preserving existing rows across schema changes
Session 3 decoupled notification delivery by adding Celery/Redis worker tasks triggered only on a status transition to 'completed' via .delay(), keeping the HTTP handler synchronous
Session 4 extracted a repository pattern (BaseRepository/TaskRepository/UserRepository) removing all SQL from route handlers

Session 5 added Flask-Limiter with a JWT-aware key function (user vs IP) plus Redis primary storage with in-memory fallback so tests run without a live broker, and redesigned GET /tasks to a cursor-paginated envelope
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically across the five sessions. The story moved from a bare CRUD API (5 tests) through ownership-scoped JWT auth (8 tests) and async Celery notifications (10 tests), to a clean repository-layer refactor (10 tests) and a rate-limited, paginated, production-flavored API (17 tests), with all tests green at every commit. The agent consistently preserved behavior during refactors (noting it kept the old list return type in Session 5 to avoid an internal API break), demonstrated increasing architectural sophistication, and layered each new concern on a stable foundation, with the only real dip being session 4's committed runtime artifacts and a couple of latent correctness wrinkles (status vocabulary, cursor-ordering mismatch) that never surfaced as regressions.
story_review.summary: A textbook, tightly-coupled five-session arc — CRUD → auth/ownership → async integration → layering refactor → cross-cutting hardening — that steadily improved in quality and finished with a clean, well-tested, feature-complete API.
